# SK5009 — An XML reader that parses a DTD and fetches what it names

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

DTD processing plus a resolver that goes to the network or the disk is XXE.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Security |
| Default severity | error |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.1 |

## Why

A DTD can declare an entity whose value is a URI, and a reader with a resolver will go and get it — so a document the process was merely asked to parse can read any file that process can read and reach any host it can reach, and hand the contents back inside the parsed result or out through an error message. That is XXE, and it turns an XML endpoint into a file-read and a request-forgery primitive at once. Two settings control it and either one closes the hole: `XmlResolver = null` keeps DTD parsing working for internal entities while resolving nothing external, and `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit` refuses the DTD outright, which is right when the documents are not supposed to have one. ⚠ There is no fix, because which of those two is correct depends on whether the documents legitimately carry a DTD — a question about the data, not about the code.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var settings = new XmlReaderSettings {
    DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Parse,
    XmlResolver = new XmlUrlResolver()
};
```

Write:

```csharp
var settings = new XmlReaderSettings {
    DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Prohibit,
    XmlResolver = null
};
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ The rule needs two facts where docs/plan/08's sentence named one, and the platform is why. On .NET Framework `DtdProcessing = DtdProcessing.Parse` was enough, because the default `XmlResolver` was an `XmlUrlResolver`. On .NET Core and later the default resolver is `null`, so parsing a DTD resolves nothing external and is not XXE — a rule that fired on `DtdProcessing.Parse` alone would report, at `error` severity, every program that legitimately parses a document with entity declarations, on a platform where that is not a vulnerability. So the rule fires only where the resolver is put back *and* the DTD is parsed. Both assignments must be explicit, both must be about the same object, and both must be in the same method: a resolver assigned from a variable is silence, because whether that variable is null is a question about another method, and `XmlSecureResolver` is excluded by name because it is the mitigation. The cost of the strictness is coverage — the shape occurs zero times in either reference tree. ⚠ Known gap, stated rather than hidden: `XmlDocument` and `XmlDataDocument` have an `XmlResolver` and no `DtdProcessing`, so the two-fact rule cannot see them and they are outside it; closing that needs its own id rather than a widening of this one.

## Configuration
